section.title: The Oracle against Tyre
section.sectionRationale: This closes the long gallery of oracles against the nations, chapters 13 to 23, with Tyre, the great Phoenician trading power whose wealth and pride made her the merchant of the nations. Her fall humbles maritime commerce itself, yet the oracle ends with a startling promise: after seventy years, Tyre's profits will be consecrated to the LORD rather than merely hoarded.
section.thesis: The LORD who planned Tyre's humbling, to strip the pride of a city that made merchandise its glory, will also, after seventy years, turn that same wealth toward His own purposes, showing that even commerce and trade can finally be brought under His lordship.
section.frameNote: Four movements: the wailing ships and the news of Tyre's ruin; the LORD's deliberate plan to disgrace the renowned of the earth; a glance at Chaldea's own earlier ruin at Assyria's hand; and the promise that after seventy years Tyre's restored profit will be set apart to the LORD.

units.label: Wail, O ships of Tarshish
units.note: the merchant of the nations laid waste

verses.text: This is the burden against Tyre: Wail, O ships of Tarshish, for Tyre is laid waste, without house or harbor. Word has reached them from the land of Cyprus.
Be silent, O dwellers of the coastland, you merchants of Sidon, whose traders have crossed the sea.
On the great waters came the grain of Shihor; the harvest of the Nile was the revenue of Tyre; she was the merchant of the nations.
Be ashamed, O Sidon, the stronghold of the sea, for the sea has spoken: “I have not been in labor or given birth. I have not raised young men or brought up young women.”
When the report reaches Egypt, they will writhe in agony over the news of Tyre.

units.label: Who planned this against Tyre? The LORD planned it

verses.text: Cross over to Tarshish; wail, O inhabitants of the coastland!
Is this your jubilant city, whose origin is from antiquity, whose feet have taken her to settle far away?
Who planned this against Tyre, the bestower of crowns, whose traders are princes, whose merchants are renowned on the earth?
The LORD of Hosts planned it, to defile all its glorious beauty, to disgrace all the renowned of the earth.
Cultivate your land like the Nile, O Daughter of Tarshish; there is no longer a harbor.
The LORD has stretched out His hand over the sea; He has made kingdoms tremble. He has given a command that the strongholds of Canaan be destroyed.
He said, “You shall rejoice no more, O oppressed Virgin Daughter of Sidon. Get up and cross over to Cyprus, even there you will find no rest.”

units.label: Look at the Chaldeans, ruined before her

verses.text: Look at the land of the Chaldeans, a people now of no account. The Assyrians destined it for the desert creatures; they set up their siege towers and stripped its palaces. They brought it to ruin.
Wail, O ships of Tarshish, for your harbor has been destroyed!

units.label: Seventy years, then restored, her profit set apart to the LORD

verses.text: At that time Tyre will be forgotten for seventy years, the span of a king's life. But at the end of seventy years, it will happen to Tyre as in the song of the harlot:
“Take up your harp, stroll through the city, O forgotten harlot. Make sweet melody, sing many a song, so you will be remembered.”
And at the end of seventy years, the LORD will restore Tyre. Then she will return to hire as a {{zanah|prostitute}} and sell herself to all the kingdoms on the face of the earth.
Yet her {{sachar|profits}} and wages will be set apart to the LORD; they will not be stored or saved, for her profit will go to those who live before the LORD, for abundant food and fine clothing.

sachar.gloss: Trade, merchandise, or the profit gained through commerce. Tyre's whole identity was built on sachar; the oracle's final surprise is that this same profit, once devoted only to accumulating wealth, will one day be set apart to the LORD instead.

zanah.gloss: To act as a prostitute, or by extension to sell oneself indiscriminately for gain. Tyre's aggressive, morally indiscriminate pursuit of trade with every nation is pictured as prostitution, yet even this profit, the oracle says, will eventually be consecrated to God rather than merely hoarded.

basic.context: Tyre was the great Phoenician trading city whose ships and merchants dominated Mediterranean commerce, so wealthy and renowned that her traders were called princes. This oracle announces her sudden humbling, sending shockwaves as far as Egypt and the Nile delta that depended on her trade, and closes the long collection of oracles against the nations that began in chapter 13.
basic.hermeneutics: This describes a real, historically anchored judgment on Tyre's pride in her wealth and trading empire, likely fulfilled in stages, including a thirteen year siege by Nebuchadnezzar and later conquest by Alexander the Great. The seventy years and Tyre's eventual restored trade being set apart to the LORD, verses 15 to 18, describes an actual, if partial, historical renewal of Tyre's commerce rather than a purely symbolic promise, while also anticipating the wider biblical hope of the nations' wealth serving God's purposes.
basic.originalLanguages: Tyre's entire identity rests on sachar, trade and profit, the word used throughout this oracle for her commercial glory. Her relentless pursuit of profit with every nation is described using the verb zanah, to prostitute oneself, yet astonishingly the oracle ends by saying this same profit will finally be set apart to the LORD rather than merely accumulated for herself.
basic.typology: Tyre's wealth finally being consecrated to the LORD rather than hoarded anticipates the New Testament's vision of the nations' glory and wealth being brought into the New Jerusalem, Revelation 21:24-26, commerce and craftsmanship redeemed for God's purposes rather than mere self-enrichment.
basic.christ: Tyre's aggressive, morally indiscriminate pursuit of wealth is judged, yet even her profit is finally destined to serve the LORD's people, a small preview of the greater gospel truth that Christ redeems and redirects even what was once given to selfish or corrupt purposes, so that the wealth of the nations ultimately serves and glorifies God, Revelation 21:24-26.
basic.god: God is sovereign over international trade and commerce, not merely armies and kings; He deliberately planned Tyre's humbling to disgrace pride that exalted itself as the renowned merchant of the nations. Yet His purposes do not end in mere destruction; He intends, after judgment, to draw even worldly wealth into service of His own people and worship.
basic.crossReferences: Ezekiel 26 to 28 gives an extended companion oracle against Tyre, detailing her pride and fall in much greater depth. Matthew 15:21-28 shows Jesus ministering near Tyre and Sidon, extending grace to a woman from this very region. Revelation 18 echoes Tyre's merchant imagery in describing Babylon's commercial fall. Revelation 21:24-26 pictures the nations' wealth and glory finally brought into the New Jerusalem.
basic.oneStory: Tyre's proud, self-serving wealth is humbled by the LORD's design, yet even this judgment is not the last word; her restored profit is destined to be set apart for God's people. This anticipates the larger biblical hope that the wealth and skill of every nation, redeemed rather than destroyed, will finally serve and glorify God through Christ.

context.literary:
Isaiah 23 is organized by a single command, 'Wail,' which is repeated in verses 1, 6 and 14. The first and last occurrences are almost identical, 'Wail, O ships of Tarshish,' and both give the reason in the same breath, the harbor is gone. That makes verses 1 to 14 a closed unit, and the final four verses, which begin 'At that time,' are a deliberate coda that changes the key.

Inside the frame the chapter works like a series of waves. Verses 1 to 5 carry the news outward, from Cyprus to the coastland to Sidon and then to Egypt, where the report of Tyre's fall will make people writhe. Verses 6 to 9 ask the question that the first five verses have raised, 'Who planned this against Tyre?', and give the answer in one short sentence of declaration, 'The LORD of Hosts planned it.' The question and answer are at the center of the chapter, and the rest of it is shaped around them. Verses 10 to 12 turn to the instrument, the LORD's stretched-out hand, and to the consequence, that even a refuge in Cyprus will bring no rest. Verses 13 and 14 hold up Babylon as a lesson.

Tyre and Sidon are addressed almost interchangeably, because they were twin Phoenician powers. The oppressed 'Virgin Daughter of Sidon' in verse 12 and the 'Daughter of Tarshish' in verse 10 are personifications of cities, a common prophetic device. Verse 4 puts words in the mouth of the sea itself, and the sea speaks as a bereaved mother who has nothing left to show, no young men, no young women.

The chapter also closes the whole gallery of oracles against the nations that opened in Isaiah 13. After Babylon, Assyria, Philistia, Moab, Damascus, Cush, Egypt, the desert peoples and Jerusalem, Tyre stands last. Several of the preceding oracles end with a turn toward the LORD's own people or toward His worship, such as Isaiah 14:32, 18:7 and 19:23-25. Isaiah 23 ends the same way, and it ends with money.
context.historical:
Tyre sat on an island fortress just off the Lebanese coast, with a mainland suburb and two harbors, and was part of a Phoenician network that included Sidon and colonies across the Mediterranean. The people of the coast were the Canaanites of the Old Testament, and the word for a merchant in Hebrew is the same as the word for Canaanite, so that Isaiah's phrase 'the merchant of the nations,' verse 3, is itself a play on her people's name. Her ships reached Tarshish, whose location is debated though most look to Spain, and Cyprus, which the BSB footnote identifies as the Hebrew Kittim.

Tyre had been a friend of Israel at the height of her power. Hiram supplied David with cedar and craftsmen, 2 Samuel 5:11, and later Solomon, who traded timber for food and gold, 1 Kings 5:1 and 9:11-14. Hiram blessed 'the LORD, the God of Israel, who made the heavens and the earth,' 2 Chronicles 2:12, and his fleet sailed with Solomon's, 1 Kings 10:22. The relationship soured. Amos charges Tyre with delivering a whole congregation of exiles to Edom and breaking 'a covenant of brotherhood,' Amos 1:9, and Joel with selling Judah's people to the Greeks, Joel 3:6. Ahab married Jezebel, the daughter of the Sidonian king, and imported Baal worship, 1 Kings 16:31.

The oracle's own history is layered. Tyre was repeatedly pressed by the great powers. Some link verses 1 and 12 with Assyrian pressure on the coast around 701 BC and the flight of her king to Cyprus. Ezekiel, writing later, says that Nebuchadnezzar brought down the walls and later notes that his army 'received no wages from Tyre,' Ezekiel 26:7 and 29:18, which implies a long and costly siege. In 332 BC Alexander the Great took the island by building a causeway to it, which fits Ezekiel 26:4, 'make her a bare rock.' The seventy years of verse 15 are discussed below. The trade restarted: under Persian rule Tyrians were again floating cedar to Joppa, Ezra 3:7.
context.canonical:
The most extended companion to this oracle is Ezekiel 26 to 28. Ezekiel 26 pictures the nations coming up like waves and Tyre made a bare rock, Ezekiel 27 is a funeral song over a great merchant ship, and Ezekiel 28 turns to the ruler of Tyre who says 'I am a god' and then to the king of Tyre in Eden, 'full of wisdom and perfect in beauty,' Ezekiel 28:2 and 28:12-13. Pride is the center of both prophets' charge, and Isaiah 23:9 states it as the LORD's own purpose, 'to disgrace all the renowned of the earth.'

The oracle is the working out of an earlier warning in the book. The Day of the LORD, Isaiah 2:12, was to come against all that is proud and lofty, and the list ends 'against every ship of Tarshish,' Isaiah 2:16. Isaiah 23 is that day falling on Tarshish's trading partner. Zechariah 9:3-4 is a later echo, with Tyre heaping silver like dust and her wealth cast into the sea.

The happier thread of the chapter is picked up elsewhere. Psalm 87:4 counts Tyre among the nations 'born in Zion,' and Psalm 45:12 has the daughter of Tyre bringing a gift to the king. Isaiah 60:5-9 pictures the riches of the sea coming to Zion, with 'the ships of Tarshish in the lead' bringing children home with silver and gold. Micah 4:13 says the wealth of many peoples will be devoted to the LORD, and Isaiah 61:6 says God's people will feed on the wealth of nations.

In the New Testament Jesus mentions Tyre and Sidon as places that would have repented, Matthew 11:21-22 and Luke 10:13-14. He visited their region, Mark 7:24, and their people came to hear Him, Mark 3:8 and Luke 6:17. Paul stayed with believers in Tyre for a week, Acts 21:3-4. Revelation 18 recasts Tyre's merchant mourning for the commerce of the final Babylon, Revelation 18:11-19.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Isaiah's task is to show a nervous Judah that the greatest economic power in the known world was neither a model nor a refuge. Tyre looked unbeatable. Her ships were everywhere, her merchants were treated as princes, and her island seemed to defy any army. Judah's leaders, who were looking for allies and trade partners as Assyria pressed, could easily have wondered whether to bind themselves to her. The oracle says that Tyre's fall is not a failure of strategy but a plan of the LORD of Hosts, and that the plan has a target: pride, the confidence that wealth is its own security.

The prophet also wants Judah to see that the nations are not merely tools or targets. The coda gives Tyre a future. She will be forgotten and then restored, and her profits will serve those who live before the LORD. Judah is invited to see her neighbors as people whom God intends to draw in, and to hold their own money more lightly in the meantime.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter does not give a policy on trade, business or banking, and it does not say that merchants are wicked. The ordinary exchange of goods is not what it condemns. What it condemns is a city whose identity and confidence rest on commerce so completely that she can 'sell herself' to every kingdom, verse 17. The harlot image is a verdict on Tyre's way of dealing with the nations and not a command to treat any group of people with contempt. The prophecy of verse 18 describes what the LORD will do with the proceeds, 'not stored or saved,' for food and clothing, and it is not a tax code or a rule for believers' finances.

What carries forward is the principle. Wealth is held under the LORD, who owns the silver and the gold, Haggai 2:8. Believers are told not to put their hope in uncertain wealth but in God, and to be generous and ready to share, 1 Timothy 6:17-19, and that is where Isaiah's picture of profit that goes to the people of God finds its application.

debates.question: How should the 'seventy years' of verse 15 be read?

views.label: A literal period of eclipse
views.case: Tyre was repeatedly subjugated, by Assyria and then by Babylon, and some take the seventy years as a real stretch of reduced trade followed by recovery. Jeremiah 25:11-12 and 29:10 give a seventy-year period to Babylon's dominance, and Tyre's eclipse is read as overlapping it, with the trade resuming under Persia, Ezra 3:7.

views.label: A lifetime, a round figure
views.case: The text itself glosses the number as 'the span of a king's life.' Psalm 90:10 treats seventy years as the length of a human life. On this reading the number says that the forgetting will last one full human generation, long enough to be felt and short enough to end.

views.label: The dominion of a single empire
views.case: Jeremiah 27:7 says the nations will serve Nebuchadnezzar, his son and his grandson until his own time comes. Some connect the 'king' of verse 15 with this single dynasty, so that Tyre's seventy years lie under the Babylonian crown.

debates.bearing: The text does not require an exact count, and the three readings agree on the pattern: a long eclipse, then a restoration that is real but limited. Interpreters should hold the number loosely and the pattern firmly.

debates.question: What is verse 13 saying about the Chaldeans?

views.label: A warning from Babylon's ruin
views.case: The BSB reads the verse as 'Look at the land of the Chaldeans,' a people of no account whom Assyria ruined. If Babylon, a city of such pride, could be brought down by Assyria, Tyre has no reason to think she is safe. The verse is then a historical precedent.

views.label: A comment on Babylon's origin
views.case: The older English translation, which is also defensible from the Hebrew, reads 'this people was not, until the Assyrian founded it for them that dwell in the wilderness,' and takes the verse as saying that Babylon was a latecomer whom Assyria raised up before she brought her down. The meaning is a reminder that powers are made and unmade by the LORD.

debates.bearing: The verse is one of the hardest in the chapter, and translators divide. On either reading the point is the same, that a once-great power fell, and Tyre should look at it and wail.

debates.question: How should Tyre's return to 'prostitution' be reconciled with the promise that her profit will be set apart to the LORD?

views.label: Her methods continue, but God uses the result
views.case: The text says Tyre will 'return to hire as a prostitute and sell herself to all the kingdoms,' verse 17. Nothing in the prophecy says her character is reformed. God takes the gains and redirects them, and the passage shows that He can use even compromised commerce for His purposes.

views.label: Her trade is changed in purpose
views.case: Verse 18 is a sharp contrast, 'they will not be stored or saved.' The profit that was once hoarded is now set apart, and 'set apart' is the language of holiness. The prophecy points to a real redirection, with the proceeds going to those who live before the LORD.

debates.bearing: Both readings confirm that God can claim what the world has used for selfish ends, and neither says that the old methods become holy. The tension with Deuteronomy 23:18, which forbids bringing a prostitute's wages into the house of the LORD to fulfill a vow, is a reason to read verse 18 as describing provision for people, not an offering laid on the altar.

study.originalLanguages:
The command that rings through the chapter, 'Wail,' is a plural imperative of the verb to howl, and the BSB footnote on verse 1 offers an alternative translation of the ships, 'fleet of trading ships.' The word 'ships of Tarshish' became a stock phrase for large seagoing vessels, and Isaiah 2:16 lists them among the proud things the LORD will bring low. The sailors' cry is repeated at both ends of the oracle, so that the main body of the oracle opens and closes on the same wail.

Verse 8 asks 'Who planned this against Tyre?' and verse 9 answers 'The LORD of Hosts planned it.' The verb is the one for giving counsel and forming a purpose, and its noun is the word for plan. It is the same vocabulary as Isaiah 14:26-27, 'This is the plan devised for the whole earth,' and Isaiah 19:17, where Egypt will tremble over what the LORD has planned. Tyre's merchants were famous for their counsel. Isaiah sets the counsel of the LORD against it, as Proverbs 19:21 does: 'Many plans are in a man's heart, but the purpose of the LORD will prevail.'

In verse 8 one of the Hebrew words for 'traders' is literally the word for Canaanites. Canaan could mean a merchant, as in Zephaniah 1:11 and Proverbs 31:24, because the Phoenician coast was the home of Canaan's trading peoples. In verse 11 the LORD gives a command concerning 'the strongholds of Canaan,' and the same word turns the geography into an economy. Isaiah is saying that the Canaan of the coast and the merchants of the world are one and the same.

The verb in verse 9 that the BSB renders 'defile' is the verb for profaning, treating as common what was held to be glorious. It is the opposite of the holiness vocabulary of verse 18, where the profits are 'set apart,' the word that elsewhere describes anything given to the LORD. What God profanes in verse 9 He sanctifies in verse 18. The high priest's plate, 'HOLY TO THE LORD,' Exodus 28:36, and the bells of the horses and cooking pots that Zechariah says will carry the same inscription, Zechariah 14:20-21, use that holiness language. The oracle ends by writing it over a merchant's ledger.

The phrase 'her hire,' in verses 17 and 18, uses a word for a prostitute's wages, which Deuteronomy 23:18 forbids bringing into the house of the LORD in fulfillment of a vow. Isaiah chooses that word on purpose. The profit is described in the most unclean terms the law has, and then given to the LORD's people for 'abundant food and fine clothing.' The sharpness of the paradox is the point.

Finally, verse 10 is textually uncertain. The BSB footnote notes that the Dead Sea Scrolls and some Septuagint manuscripts read 'Cultivate,' where the Masoretic Text has 'Overflow.' Translators have to choose whether Tarshish is told to farm the land like the Nile or to flood out like it.

typology.type: The ships of Tarshish, from wailing to bringing home, Isaiah 23:1 and 23:14
typology.fulfillment: The ships that Isaiah tells to wail are the same ships that later bring Zion's children home. Isaiah 60:9 says 'the ships of Tarshish in the lead' will carry 'your children from afar, with their silver and gold, to the honor of the LORD,' and Psalm 72:10-11 has the kings of Tarshish and distant shores bringing tribute. In Christ the movement reaches a new stage: the Magi bring gold and frankincense to the Child, Matthew 2:11, and the kings of the earth bring their glory into the city, Revelation 21:24. The type is still unfolding, and it falls short in a plain way, because the ships of Isaiah are instruments of a trade empire while the city of Revelation has no need of one.

typology.type: Hiram of Tyre and the building of the house, 1 Kings 5:1
typology.fulfillment: Tyre supplied cedar, craftsmen and gold for David's palace and Solomon's temple, 2 Samuel 5:11 and 1 Kings 5:1, and Hiram blessed the LORD, 2 Chronicles 2:12. A people outside the covenant helped to build the house where God would dwell. Paul says Gentiles are 'no longer strangers and foreigners' but are 'being built together into a dwelling place for God,' with Christ as the cornerstone, Ephesians 2:19-22. The correspondence is that of foreign hands in God's building. The escalation is that in Christ the Gentiles are not suppliers of material but living stones of the house itself. The type has a flaw too, since Hiram's cooperation was friendly and temporary, and the relationship later broke, Amos 1:9.

typology.type: Profit set apart, not stored, Isaiah 23:18
typology.fulfillment: Wealth that is not hoarded but flows to those who live before the LORD, for food and clothing, is the pattern of the first Christians, who sold property and laid the proceeds at the apostles' feet 'for distribution to anyone as he had need,' Acts 4:34-35. Jesus gave the teaching behind it, 'Do not store up for yourselves treasures on earth,' Matthew 6:19-21, and the pattern behind that, 'though He was rich, yet for your sakes He became poor,' 2 Corinthians 8:9. The type falls short because Isaiah describes a future arrangement for Tyre's trade, while the church's giving is voluntary and has no taxing power. The echo is a pattern, not a prediction of Acts.

typology.type: The proud ruler brought low, Isaiah 23:8-9
typology.fulfillment: Tyre's 'bestower of crowns' is humbled so that all pride before the LORD is exposed. Ezekiel spells out the same pride in the ruler who says 'I am a god,' Ezekiel 28:2. The pattern is reversed in Christ, who 'did not consider equality with God something to be grasped, but emptied Himself,' and was therefore exalted, Philippians 2:6-9. The proud are brought down and the humble are raised, and Jesus Himself is the pattern for that exchange. The correspondence is by contrast rather than likeness.

study.christ:
The oracle reaches Christ in four ways, and the first is by the direction of its ending. Isaiah ends with money flowing toward God's people, and the New Testament says that the nations will bring their glory into the city, Revelation 21:24-26. The pattern begins at the Child's cradle. The Magi came from the east and opened their treasures, offering gold and frankincense and myrrh, Matthew 2:11, as Isaiah 60:6 had pictured the nations bringing gold and frankincense and proclaiming the LORD's praise. Jesus is the focus toward which the wealth of the nations is finally drawn.

The second way is through the Gospels' own handling of Tyre and Sidon. Jesus said that Tyre and Sidon would have repented in sackcloth if they had seen what Chorazin and Bethsaida saw, Matthew 11:21-22. He went into their region, Mark 7:24, and people from there came to hear Him, Mark 3:8 and Luke 6:17. A woman of that country came to Him, and Matthew calls her a Canaanite, Matthew 15:22, using the old name of the coast, while Mark calls her Syrophoenician, Mark 7:26. Jesus said that the children are to be fed first, and she answered that even the dogs eat the crumbs, and He gave her what she asked, Mark 7:27-29. The oracle's last word about Tyre, that her gains would one day feed and clothe the LORD's people, is answered by a Tyrian-region woman who receives bread from the Lord's table.

The third way is by contrast with the pride that the oracle humbles. Tyre's glory was that she bestowed crowns. Christ is the one who did not grasp at equality with God but emptied Himself and was exalted, Philippians 2:6-9. The ruler of Tyre said, 'I am a god,' Ezekiel 28:2, and the Son who really was God became a servant.

The fourth is the Lord's own attitude to money. 'You cannot serve both God and money,' He said, Luke 16:13, and He pointed His disciples to treasure that moths cannot touch, Matthew 6:19-21. He who was rich became poor so that others might become rich, 2 Corinthians 8:9.

The chapter does not name the Messiah, and these links depend on how the New Testament itself treats Tyre, the nations' wealth and the humbling of pride. Isaiah 23:18 does not predict the church's collections, and Matthew 15 is not a fulfillment of the verse. They are the same movement, the LORD drawing the unlikely and the proud into His people, seen at its center.
study.god:
The first thing this chapter shows is that God is the author of history even where history seems to run on trade routes and treaties. When Tyre falls, the prophet does not tell us about armies. He asks, 'Who planned this against Tyre?', and answers in one line, 'The LORD of Hosts planned it,' verse 9. The same word for plan appears in Isaiah 14:26-27, 'This is the plan devised for the whole earth,' and the same thought is in Psalm 33:10-11, where the LORD frustrates the plans of nations while His own counsel stands forever. The historical instruments, Assyria, Babylon and later Alexander, go unnamed in the oracle's central verses. God does not need to be hidden behind them. He works through them.

He is Lord of the sea. 'The LORD has stretched out His hand over the sea,' verse 11, uses the language of the Exodus, when Moses stretched out his hand over the sea and the LORD drove it back, Exodus 14:21. The same hand that parted the waters for Israel makes kingdoms tremble over the waves. The sea in verse 4 is a bereaved mother, and the sea is the thing the Phoenicians thought they had mastered. God is the one who owns it.

He is jealous for glory that belongs to Him. The oracle says the plan was 'to defile all its glorious beauty, to disgrace all the renowned of the earth.' It is not merely that Tyre is punished for particular sins. The pride of being the one who gives crowns and whose merchants are princes is the offense, and God deals with it as He does with every proud and lofty thing, Isaiah 2:12-16.

He is the owner of all wealth. 'The silver is Mine, and the gold is Mine,' declares the LORD, Haggai 2:8, and 'The earth is the LORD's, and the fullness thereof,' Psalm 24:1. That ownership explains the coda. When profit is set apart to the LORD, nothing foreign has been brought into His house. His own has been returned to Him.

He holds judgment and restoration together. There are seventy years of being forgotten, and then He 'will restore Tyre,' verse 17. He is also generous with His grace across the borders, since Tyre is among the nations that Psalm 87:4 counts as born in Zion. For worship, the chapter says to hold money as His, to be wary of the pride that comes with success, and to remember that God's purposes reach to the harbors and markets of the world.

crossReferences.note: The Day of the LORD is announced against all that is proud and lofty, and the list ends with 'every ship of Tarshish.' Isaiah 23 is that day arriving at the harbor, and shows why the ships are told to wail.

The LORD's plan 'devised for the whole earth' and His outstretched hand that no one can turn back. The verbs of planning match Isaiah 23:8-9 and show the Tyre oracle as one case of a plan that covers every nation in the gallery.

Moses stretched out his hand over the sea and the LORD drove the waters back. Isaiah 23:11 uses the same gesture, the LORD stretching His hand over the sea, so that the God of the Exodus is the one who shakes the maritime power of Tyre.

Hiram of Tyre sends envoys to Solomon, as he had always been a friend of David. Tyre was not always an enemy of Israel, and the history of friendship and partnership makes the later breach and the final promise of verse 18 more poignant.

The ruler of Tyre says 'I am a god; I sit in the seat of gods in the heart of the sea,' and is told he is only a man. Ezekiel supplies in direct speech the pride that Isaiah 23:9 says the LORD planned to disgrace.

Nebuchadnezzar's army labored against Tyre until every head was bald and every shoulder raw, yet received no wages from her. It adds historical detail to the long siege behind the oracle and shows the fall was costly even for the conqueror.
Tyre is named among the nations whom the LORD will record as 'born in Zion.' The psalm shows that the oracle's coda belongs to a larger hope in which even Tyre has a place among God's people.

The wages of a prostitute may not be brought into the house of the LORD to fulfill a vow. The law's severity sharpens the paradox of Isaiah 23:17-18, where Tyre's 'hire' is set apart to the LORD, and invites careful reading of what exactly is being done with it.

The riches of the sea and the wealth of the nations come to Zion, with 'the ships of Tarshish in the lead.' The ships told to wail in Isaiah 23:1 and 23:14 become the ships that carry God's children home, and so the oracle's two halves are answered in a single image.

Zion is told that she will devote the gain of many peoples to the LORD and their wealth to the Lord of all the earth. It repeats Isaiah 23:18 in different words and shows the idea spreading across the prophets.

Jesus withdraws to the district of Tyre and Sidon and meets a Canaanite woman who cries out to the Son of David. It places the Messiah on the very coast that Isaiah addressed, and shows grace reaching people from the old Canaanite trading land.

The merchants of the earth weep because no one is left to buy their cargo, a list that begins with gold and silver and ends with 'slaves and souls of men.' The list is modeled on Tyre's own cargo in Ezekiel 27 and shows the Tyre oracle projected onto the final Babylon.

The kings of the earth bring their glory into the city, and 'the glory and honor of the nations' is brought into it. It is the New Testament's own picture of the end toward which Isaiah 23:18 is pointing.

study.oneStory:
The story of Tyre is an old one. In Genesis the sons of Canaan include Sidon his firstborn, Genesis 10:15, and the people of the coast belong to the family that Israel was told to dislodge. Yet their city sits at the edge of the story for a thousand years as a place of skill, ships and timber, and for a short, bright season as a friend. Hiram blesses the God of Israel, supplies the cedar for His house, and sails with Solomon's fleet, 2 Chronicles 2:11-12 and 1 Kings 10:22. The same Tyre is where Jezebel's father reigned, and the Baal worship that she carried into Israel is one of the great disasters of the northern kingdom, 1 Kings 16:31.

That double face is why the prophets give Tyre so much attention. She is a talented, wealthy, outward-looking culture that has everything except the fear of the LORD. In Ezekiel her king is an Eden figure whose pride throws him from the garden, Ezekiel 28:12-17, and Isaiah gives the same fall in a few words, the 'renowned of the earth' disgraced, verse 9. The world's glory, left to itself, repeats the old story of Genesis 3: a proud creature who wants to be like God.

But the oracle does not stop at the fall. It turns, and the turn is characteristic of the way the whole Bible moves. Judgment is not the last thing God does with Tyre. In the closing verses she is forgotten, restored and set apart, and her ledger is rewritten. The same turn shapes the whole gallery of oracles, where Egypt becomes 'My people,' Assyria 'My handiwork,' and Israel 'My inheritance,' Isaiah 19:25. The nations that were once enemies are drawn in.

The story's center is Christ, who withdrew to the region of Tyre and Sidon, healed a woman's daughter and let the crowds of that coast come to hear Him, Mark 7:24-30 and Luke 6:17. The church that follows had believers in Tyre within a generation, Acts 21:3-4. The end is the city in which the merchants of the earth no longer mourn, because the ships have come home. 'The glory and honor of the nations' is carried through gates that are never shut, Revelation 21:24-26, and the only commerce that remains is the gift of everything back to the God who made the sea.

quiz.q: What made Tyre so renowned before her judgment in this oracle?

options.text: Her vast maritime trade, with merchants called princes, renowned across the earth.
options.note: Verses 3 and 8 describe exactly this trading glory and renown.

options.text: Her powerful standing army and land conquests.
options.note: The oracle focuses on Tyre's commercial, maritime glory, not land-based military conquest.

options.text: Her role as a center of pagan religious pilgrimage.
options.note: Not the focus of this oracle; her fame here is specifically commercial.

options.text: Her agricultural exports of grain and wine.
options.note: Grain and produce from the Nile passed through her, verse 3, but her core identity was trade itself, not her own agriculture.

quiz.q: Who does the oracle say planned Tyre's humbling, and why?

options.text: The LORD of Hosts planned it, to disgrace all the renowned of the earth.
options.note: Verse 9 states this explicitly: the LORD planned it to humble pride.

options.text: Rival merchants from Sidon planned it out of jealousy.
options.note: The text attributes the plan to the LORD, not commercial rivals.

options.text: It happened purely by economic accident with no divine involvement.
options.note: The oracle explicitly credits the LORD's deliberate plan, not chance.

options.text: The Assyrians alone planned and carried it out.
options.note: Human armies act as instruments, but the text credits the ultimate planning to the LORD Himself.

quiz.q: What historical precedent does verse 13 point to?

options.text: The earlier ruin of the Chaldeans at the hands of the Assyrians.
options.note: Verse 13 explicitly recalls the Chaldeans being reduced to ruin by Assyria as a precedent.

options.text: The destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah.
options.note: Not mentioned in this passage; the precedent given is the Chaldeans and Assyria.

options.text: The exodus from Egypt.
options.note: Not referenced in this specific verse.

options.text: The building of the first temple.
options.note: Unrelated to this verse's actual content, which recalls a nation's military ruin.

quiz.q: What happens to Tyre's profit after her seventy years of being forgotten, according to verse 18?

options.text: It will be set apart to the LORD, going to those who live before Him.
options.note: Verse 18 states this surprising redirection of Tyre's restored wealth explicitly.

options.text: It will be permanently destroyed and never recovered.
options.note: The opposite; her trade is restored and her profit redirected, not destroyed.

options.text: It will be seized entirely by the king of Babylon.
options.note: Not stated in this passage; the profit is directed toward the LORD's people, not a foreign king.

options.text: It will be equally divided among all the nations she once traded with.
options.note: The text specifies the profit serves those who live before the LORD, not an equal distribution among all nations.

quiz.q: How does Tyre's restored, consecrated wealth anticipate the New Testament?

options.text: It anticipates the nations' wealth and glory being brought into the New Jerusalem.
options.note: Revelation 21:24-26 pictures exactly this final ingathering of the nations' wealth to God's glory.

options.text: It shows that all wealth is inherently evil and must be destroyed.
options.note: The opposite; this oracle envisions wealth redeemed and redirected, not simply destroyed.

options.text: It has no connection to any New Testament theme.
options.note: There is a clear thematic link to Revelation's vision of the nations' wealth serving God's glory.

options.text: It refers only to Tyre's literal ancient economy with no further significance.
options.note: The historical fulfillment is real, but Scripture also draws forward theological significance from this pattern of redeemed wealth.

questions: Tyre's identity and pride were built entirely on her wealth and trade. What achievement, possession, or reputation do you build your own identity on more than you should?
The LORD deliberately planned to disgrace all the renowned of the earth. Where do you see pride, your own or a system you are part of, that God may be working to humble?

Tyre's profit, once pursued indiscriminately, was finally set apart to the LORD. What resources, skills, or income do you have that could be more deliberately dedicated to God's purposes rather than only your own?
Jesus later ministered with grace to a woman from Tyre and Sidon's region. Who in your life feels as far outside God's reach as ancient Tyre, and how might God be inviting you to extend grace there?
This oracle shows that even judged, compromised systems can be redeemed for God's purposes. Where do you need hope that a broken situation in your own life is not beyond God's redemptive power?

translationNotes.note: Tarshish likely refers to a distant western trading port, possibly in Spain, representing the far reach of Tyre's maritime trade network.
Seventy years likely parallels the length of Judah's own Babylonian exile.
